This is my account of the Saturday delivery to Riverbend Market, stall fourteen. The market opens at seven, but the unloading lane is meant to be clear by 6:20. The delivery was booked for 5:40 on the ninth of June, and it carried herbs, tomatoes, bread, and the folding display boards. I was at the stall from 5:15 with Mara, the market coordinator, and Dev, who runs the stall. The forecast said light rain after eight, not before dawn, and the ground was already wet from the night before, so we put the rubber mats beside the curb instead of under the crates.

The van arrived at 5:52, driven by Rosa from North Quay Produce. She had the usual green delivery sheet and a separate bakery docket because the bread came from a different supplier. The van could not turn into the lane because a catering truck had stopped across the entrance. Rosa waited by the loading sign while Dev went to wake the caretaker at the bakery door. At 5:58, the truck moved, but the van had to reverse once because a stack of empty fish boxes narrowed the turn. Mara asked whether we wanted her to call the market office, and I said, “No, we can finish unloading before the first customers arrive.”

Rosa counted six blue crates of tomatoes and four shallow boxes of herbs. She read the labels aloud as she checked them. Two crates were marked salad tomatoes and four were cooking tomatoes. The herb boxes held parsley, mint, and coriander, but there was no basil on the sheet or in the van. Dev looked at the order on his phone and said, “Basil was on the change I sent on Thursday.” Rosa checked her messages and said she had the change, but the warehouse had not picked it. She did not pretend it was on the delivery, and she wrote a shortage note beside the item.

I had seen the change arrive, and I said, “Right, that is the Thursday message, and it asks for two bunches, not two boxes.” That “right” was me confirming the message, not me agreeing that basil had been delivered. Mara looked at the screen and confirmed the quantity: two bunches. We agreed to keep the line open on the sheet until Dev could call the supplier after opening. The basil was for a prepared herb mix, and the stall could sell the other herbs separately, so it was a problem but not a reason to refuse the rest of the load.

The bakery docket listed thirty-two rolls and twelve rye loaves. The roll count was right, but there were only ten rye loaves on the trolley. Rosa checked the van again while I checked under the folded cloth and inside the bread trays. There were no more loaves. Dev said, “Please record ten received and two missing. I need the count to match what we pay for.” Rosa wrote ten beside “rye loaves” and asked Dev to initial the docket. He did that at 6:12 and took a photo for his shop records.

Mara asked me to note the condition of the produce before we put it on the display. Here is the list:
1. The tomato crates were dry underneath, and the fruit was firm with no split skins.
2. The parsley and coriander were cool and damp but not dripping.
3. The mint box had a crushed corner, and three stems were pressed flat near the lid.
4. One wooden slat on the bottom blue crate was loose, but it did not touch the tomatoes.
5. The paper bread bags were dry, and the rye loaves had no torn wrapping.

Rosa offered to replace the mint stems on her afternoon run, but she could not replace them during this delivery.

We set the herbs on the upper shelf so the mint would not be squeezed by the bread. The tomatoes stayed on the lower rack, and Dev moved the crate with the loose slat onto a plastic tray. He said he would ask his brother to repair the crate after closing. I nearly wrote that the tray belonged to the market—no, the tray belonged to Dev, and he had brought it from the stall storeroom. I crossed out my first wording before anyone signed the condition note. Mara said the loose slat was worth recording even if the produce looked fine, because a second delivery might stack another load on top of that crate.

At 6:23, Rosa handed over the green delivery sheet and the bakery docket. Dev signed for the quantities that had arrived, but not for the missing basil or the two rye loaves. Mara signed only as the person who witnessed the count. She did not approve a credit or promise a replacement. Rosa said the supplier office would review the shortage notes once the paperwork reached them. Dev asked whether the bread could be credited before the market closed. Rosa said she could not give him an answer and told him to keep the photograph with his copy.

The main condition is that if the basil arrives on the afternoon run, Dev wants it brought straight to stall fourteen before three, because the herb mix is prepared at 3:30. If it does not arrive, he will make a smaller mix with parsley and mint and will not put coriander into that recipe. I wrote the condition on the back of the delivery sheet, and Dev read it before he left the bay. He said, “Yes, before three if it comes; otherwise, we adjust the mix.” Mara took a picture of that note so the office could see the timing.

After the van left, we swept the damp leaves from the curb and put the empty crates behind the stall, not in the public walkway. The market office called at 6:31 to ask why the catering truck had blocked the lane. Mara gave them the time and the vehicle description but did not make a complaint on Dev’s behalf. He had already told the catering driver where to park next time. The stall opened on schedule. The first customer arrived while Dev was arranging the tomatoes, and I finished the note by listing the confirmed counts, the two shortages, and the loose crate slat.

The box wording may have come from an older room list, which uses “box” as a general storage term, but there is no separate box with these items. Please correct the draft rather than making a second location entry. The folder and tapes are together now, and I did not move them while checking the first three files.

Please include the note about the sound gap on tape two and the conflicting room labels for tape three, keeping my uncertainty about both matters clear. The first three files are the only ones I have listened to so far; I have not reviewed the remaining fifteen transfers or listened to any of the cassettes. That is the present extent of my review, and the packet should reflect it.

The crew should not reopen zone 4 just to see whether the pressure returns; doing so before the repair could send water into the excavation area. The plan is to keep that zone isolated while digging and to keep the rest of the block on its normal schedule unless the filter-house gauge falls below 45 psi. The valve was stiff during the first attempt, but it did close, and no one has tested it again under pressure. Use the replacement valve only if the old one fails that check, not simply because the replacement is already on site.

2. Check the valve and inspect the pipe and both sides of the wet joint before cutting. Photograph the exposed connection beside a ruler for the maintenance record.
